After a customer is inserted on day 1, subsequent days should update them. The MERGE has no update clause — but that only means updates are silently ignored, not that duplicates are created. Look at what's unique about the source files themselves.

title: Adaptive Query Execution: skew join optimisation mechanism
description: With `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true` and `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`, Spark detects that one shuffle partition in a sort-merge join is 500× larger than the median. How does AQE's skew join optimisation handle this at runtime?
code_snippet:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled', 'true')

result = orders.join(line_items, on='order_id')
options: AQE splits the skewed partition into N sub-partitions and replicates the corresponding partition from the other side of the join N times, allowing N parallel tasks to process the skewed key — each processing 1/N of the hot partition against a full copy of the matching other-side data; the final results are union-ed together
AQE switches the skewed partition to a broadcast join at runtime, sending the smaller side of that partition to every executor so the large partition can be processed locally without a shuffle
AQE re-hashes the skewed partition using a secondary hash function on a different key column, distributing rows more evenly across new partitions before the join executes
AQE detects the skewed partition and quarantines it for a second-pass join after the main join completes, ensuring the skewed rows don't delay the non-skewed partitions from finishing
explanation: AQE's skew join optimisation works by splitting a skewed partition and replicating the corresponding partition from the other join side. Concretely: if shuffle partition 42 from the orders side has 500× the median data, AQE splits it into N sub-partitions (based on a skew factor threshold). For each sub-partition, it replicates partition 42 from the line_items side. Now N tasks process the skewed data in parallel — each task handles 1/N of the hot orders partition joined against all matching line_items for those orders. The sub-results are union-ed. This is entirely transparent to the user and requires no code change; it activates based on runtime shuffle statistics collected after the shuffle write stage completes. The total data processed is slightly higher due to replication, but the wall-clock time is dramatically lower.
hints: AQE can observe actual partition sizes after the shuffle write stage completes, before the join read stage begins. With that information, it can restructure the join plan for the skewed partition specifically — without touching the non-skewed partitions.

Think about what it means to 'split' a large partition and join it in parallel. If you split the left side into 4 sub-parts, what must happen to the corresponding right-side partition to ensure each sub-task still gets all matching rows?

title: Structured Streaming watermark dropping legitimate late events
description: A Structured Streaming job aggregates clickstream events by 5-minute tumbling windows. A 15-minute watermark is configured to allow for late data. However, the ops team reports that events arriving 8 minutes late are being dropped. Examine the code and metrics to identify the cause.
code_snippet:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

streamDf = spark.readStream \
    .format('kafka') \
    .option('kafka.bootstrap.servers', 'kafka:9092') \
    .option('subscribe', 'clickstream') \
    .load()

parsed = streamDf.select(
    F.from_json(F.col('value').cast('string'), schema).alias('data')
).select('data.*')

aggDf = parsed \
    .withWatermark('processing_time', '15 minutes') \
    .groupBy(F.window('event_time', '5 minutes')) \
    .agg(F.count('*').alias('clicks'))

aggDf.writeStream.outputMode('append').format('delta') \
    .option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/clicks').start()
scenario_context:
Event pipeline timestamps (2024-03-14):
  Kafka message produce time:     14:00:00 UTC
  Event actual occurrence time:   13:52:00 UTC  (8 min before produce time)

Spark Streaming query state:
  Current watermark:    derived from max(processing_time) - 15 min
  Window 13:50–13:55:   DROPPED at 14:08 (8 min after first message for this window)

Watermark events log:
  14:00:00  processing_time high watermark = 14:00:00
  14:00:00  watermark threshold = 14:00:00 - 15min = 13:45:00
  14:00:00  Window 13:50–13:55 end = 13:55 < watermark 13:45? NO — window retained
  14:08:00  processing_time high watermark = 14:08:00
  14:08:00  watermark threshold = 14:08 - 15min = 13:53:00
  14:08:00  Window 13:50–13:55 end = 13:55 < watermark 13:53? YES — window CLOSED
options: The watermark is applied to `processing_time` (the time the message was received by Spark) rather than `event_time` (when the click actually occurred). The watermark progresses based on the latest processing time seen, not the latest event time — so as micro-batches run, processing_time advances quickly and closes windows based on wall-clock time, not event occurrence time. Events 8 minutes late in event time but processed promptly are dropped because the processing_time watermark has already advanced past the window boundary.

The 15-minute watermark is too short for a 5-minute window — Spark requires the watermark to be at least 3× the window duration (15 min) to allow correct late-data handling; increase the watermark to 20 minutes to account for the window duration

In 'append' output mode, Spark finalises and outputs a window only after the watermark passes the window end time. The 8-minute-late events arrive before the watermark closes the window at 13:45 — they should be included. The actual issue is a Kafka consumer lag of 8 minutes causing events to arrive after their window should have been emitted

The watermark configuration is correct; the events are being dropped by the Kafka deserialisation layer because the `from_json` schema does not include a field for events older than the current micro-batch processing time
explanation: The bug is `withWatermark('processing_time', '15 minutes')`. Watermarks are designed to be applied to the event time column used in the window groupBy — in this case, `event_time`. By applying it to `processing_time`, the watermark advances based on when Spark processes messages, not when the events occurred. As each micro-batch runs, `processing_time` advances rapidly (near wall clock time), causing the watermark threshold to rise quickly. A 5-minute window ending at 13:55 is closed once the watermark exceeds 13:55, which happens just 8 minutes into processing. Events with `event_time=13:52` arrive after the window closes — not because they are late relative to event time, but because the wrong timestamp column is driving watermark progress. The fix: `withWatermark('event_time', '15 minutes')` — the watermark should track the maximum seen event time, not processing time.
hints: The watermark's job is to track how far behind the event timeline Spark is willing to wait. If the timestamp column driving the watermark is not the same column used in the window groupBy, what is the watermark actually measuring?

Look at the watermark log: the threshold advances to 13:53 within 8 minutes of wall-clock time. Real events are only 8 minutes late in event-time — but the watermark is not tracking event-time at all. What column determines how fast the watermark advances here?

title: Dynamic partition pruning: when does it activate?
description: You run a star-schema query joining a 2TB fact table (`orders`, partitioned by `order_date`) with a dimension filter on a 500MB `promotions` table. AQE is enabled. Under which condition does Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP) activate to skip irrelevant fact table partitions at scan time?
code_snippet:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled', 'true')

result = orders.join(
    promotions.filter(F.col('campaign') == 'SUMMER2024'),
    on='promotion_id'
)
result.groupBy('region').agg(F.sum('amount')).show()
options: DPP activates when the fact table is partitioned on the join key (`promotion_id`) — Spark injects the result of the dimension-side filter as a subquery into the fact table scan, using partition metadata to skip partitions whose `promotion_id` values are not in the filtered dimension set, avoiding reading the full 2TB table

DPP activates whenever AQE is enabled and the dimension table is under the broadcast join threshold; the pruning is performed during the broadcast hash build phase and applies to any column in the fact table scan

DPP activates when the fact table and dimension table share the same sort order on the join key — Spark can then use a binary search on partition boundaries to skip non-matching ranges without a subquery injection

DPP activates automatically for any join involving a partitioned table; the optimiser statically analyses the filter predicates at plan compile time and determines which partitions to skip before the job starts
explanation:
DPP injects the filtered dimension result as a runtime subquery filter on the fact table's partition column, but only when the join key matches the fact table's partition key. Here, `orders` is partitioned by `order_date`, not by `promotion_id` — so DPP cannot prune `order_date` partitions based on a `promotion_id` filter. For DPP to activate, `orders` would need to be partitioned by `promotion_id`. When that condition is met, Spark evaluates the filtered dimension side, collects its `promotion_id` values, and injects a `promotion_id IN (...)` condition into the fact table's partition scan — reading only matching partitions.

Option B describes the broadcast-reuse default (`reuseBroadcastOnly=true`) but conflates the optimization with the DPP mechanism itself — DPP fundamentally works via subquery injection; broadcast reuse is a configurable performance optimization (avoids running an extra dimension scan when a broadcast is already happening), not a mechanism requirement. Option B also incorrectly says DPP applies to any column in the fact table scan — DPP only prunes the physical partition column.

Option C is wrong: DPP does not work by sort-order alignment; it injects a runtime IN-list filter.

Option D is wrong: DPP requires the join-key-to-partition-column match, not just any partitioned table.
hints: Dynamic Partition Pruning works by using the filtered dimension table result to eliminate entire fact table partitions at scan time. For that to work, the partition metadata must correspond to the join key — what must the fact table be partitioned on?

In this query, `orders` is partitioned by `order_date` but the join is on `promotion_id`. Can Spark use the set of filtered promotion IDs to skip `order_date` partitions? What would need to change about the partitioning scheme?

title: Predict schema: nullability after arithmetic on a non-nullable column
description: A DataFrame is created with an explicit schema where `salary` is declared non-nullable. After a `withColumn` that performs arithmetic on it, what does `printSchema()` show for the new column's nullability?
code_snippet:
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, LongType, StringType

schema = StructType([
    StructField('emp_id', StringType(), nullable=True),
    StructField('salary', LongType(), nullable=False),  # declared non-nullable
])
df = spark.createDataFrame([('E001', 90000), ('E002', 120000)], schema)
result = df.withColumn('salary_bumped', df['salary'] * 1.1)
result.printSchema()
options:
root
 |-- emp_id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- salary: long (nullable = false)
 |-- salary_bumped: double (nullable = false)  (non-nullable input → non-nullable output)

root
 |-- emp_id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- salary: long (nullable = false)
 |-- salary_bumped: double (nullable = true)  (Spark marks all computed columns nullable = true regardless of input nullability)

root
 |-- emp_id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- salary: long (nullable = false)
 |-- salary_bumped: long (nullable = false)  (multiplication preserves both type and non-nullable flag)
AnalysisException: arithmetic on a non-nullable LongType column requires explicit casting to a nullable type first
explanation: Spark's Catalyst optimizer conservatively marks all derived (computed) columns as `nullable = true` in the output schema, even when the input columns are non-nullable. This is a deliberate design decision: Spark cannot statically prove that an expression will never produce null in all possible execution paths (e.g., division by zero with some configurations, UDFs, certain math functions on edge values). Rather than risk a null-in-non-nullable-column constraint violation at runtime, Catalyst always sets `nullable = true` for computed columns. Additionally, `salary * 1.1` promotes the LongType to DoubleType (multiplying a long by a floating-point literal), which is correctly reflected in the schema. Option A is incorrect because Spark doesn't propagate non-nullability through arithmetic. Option C is incorrect because the result type changes from Long to Double.
hints: Spark's schema for a computed expression is determined by Catalyst at plan-analysis time, not at execution time. Catalyst cannot prove that an arithmetic expression will never produce null in all circumstances — so what does it do?
Notice that `salary * 1.1` multiplies a Long by a floating-point literal. What type promotion occurs, and how does Spark's conservative nullability policy apply to the result?

title: AQE Skew Join: How Many Tasks Process the Hot Partition?
description:
AQE is enabled with the configuration below. After the shuffle write stage completes, the probe-side output shows:
- **Partition 0:** 1,920 MB
- **Partitions 1–199:** 18 MB each (median ≈ 18 MB)

How many join tasks does AQE create **specifically for partition 0**?
code_snippet:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes", "64mb")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor", "5")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes", "256mb")

# After a shuffle stage:
# Partition 0  : 1,920 MB
# Partitions 1-199: ~18 MB each  (median = 18 MB)
options: 1 task — AQE's skew join detects the hot partition but queues it for a second-pass join after the non-skewed partitions finish; it still runs as a single task
5 tasks — the skewedPartitionFactor determines how many sub-tasks are created for each skewed partition
30 tasks — AQE splits partition 0 into ceil(1,920 MB ÷ 64 MB) = 30 sub-partitions, each processing ~64 MB; the build side is replicated once per sub-partition so every sub-task has all matching rows
200 tasks — AQE detects skew and resets the entire shuffle to the original partition count, redistributing all data evenly before the join
explanation: AQE's skew join detects partition 0 as skewed because 1,920 MB > `skewedPartitionFactor (5) × median (18 MB) = 90 MB` AND > `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (256 MB)` — both conditions must hold. AQE then splits partition 0 into `ceil(1,920 ÷ 64) = 30` sub-partitions, each targeting `advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (64 MB)`. For each sub-partition, AQE replicates the corresponding build-side partition, so every sub-task joins its ~64 MB slice against all matching build rows. The 30 sub-tasks run in parallel, turning a single 1,920 MB bottleneck task into 30 manageable tasks. Non-skewed partitions 1–199 each run as normal single tasks. Option A is wrong — AQE splits skewed partitions at runtime; it does not queue them for a second pass. Option B is wrong — `skewedPartitionFactor` is a detection threshold multiplier (a partition must be > factor × median size to qualify as skewed), not a split count. Option D is wrong — AQE never reshuffles all data; it surgically restructures only the identified skewed partitions.
hints: skewedPartitionFactor and skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes are detection thresholds, not split counts — once a partition is identified as skewed, how does AQE decide how many pieces to cut it into?
The advisory partition size is the target size per output partition — apply that same logic to the skewed partition's total size.

title: Salted Join: What Does result.count() Return?
description:
`df_events` has **40,000 rows**, all with `user_id = 'bot'`. `df_users` has **1 row** with `user_id = 'bot'`.

A salted join is applied to distribute the hot key. What does `result.count()` return?
code_snippet:
N_SALT = 8

# Large side: assign each row a random salt 0–7
df_events_salted = (
    df_events
    .withColumn("_salt", (F.rand() * N_SALT).cast("int"))
    .withColumn("uid_s", F.concat(F.col("user_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("_salt")))
)

# Small side: explode to produce one copy per salt value
df_users_salted = (
    df_users
    .withColumn("_salts", F.array([F.lit(i) for i in range(N_SALT)]))
    .select("*", F.explode("_salts").alias("_salt"))
    .withColumn("uid_s", F.concat(F.col("user_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("_salt")))
)

result = df_events_salted.join(df_users_salted, on="uid_s", how="inner")
result.count()
options: 320,000 — the 8-way explode on the users side multiplies every match: 40,000 events × 8 salt copies = 320,000 output rows
40,000 — each event row carries one salt value 0–7 and joins to exactly the one users row that was exploded to the same salt; the distribution spreads load but does not multiply output cardinality
8 — after the join, rows are collapsed to one per salt bucket since all events in a bucket share the same salted key
0 — rand() produces floats in [0.0, 1.0) so casting to int always yields 0, but the users side has salts 1–7 for that bucket, producing no matches
explanation: Salting distributes a hot key across N partitions without multiplying output cardinality. Each event row is assigned one salt value (0–7 via `(rand() * 8).cast(int)`), producing a unique `uid_s` such as `'bot_3'`. The users side is exploded from 1 row into 8 rows (`'bot_0'` through `'bot_7'`). The inner join on `uid_s` matches each event row to exactly the one users row sharing its salt — `'bot_3'` matches only `'bot_3'`, not all 8. Result: 40,000 events × 1 matching user per event = 40,000 rows. Option A is the classic misunderstanding: the explode creates 8 small-side copies so that every possible salt value has a join partner, but a given event row with salt=3 cannot match the users row with salt=5. Option C is wrong — the join does not aggregate; all 40,000 individual rows are preserved. Option D is wrong — `(rand() * 8).cast(int)` yields integers 0 through 7 uniformly; rand() returns [0.0, 1.0) so the product spans [0.0, 8.0) and casts produce 0–7 inclusive.
hints: Each event row carries exactly one salt value. How many users rows share that same salt value after the explode?
The explode on the small side ensures every possible salt has a join partner — it does not mean every event matches multiple users rows.

title: Watermark Boundary: Which Incoming Events Are Dropped?
description:
A Structured Streaming job runs in Append output mode with a **10-minute watermark** on `event_time`.

The previous micro-batch's maximum observed `event_time` was **14:20:00**.

The current micro-batch contains these four events:

| Event | event_time |
|---|---|
| e1 | 14:25:00 |
| e2 | 14:18:00 |
| e3 | 14:10:00 |
| e4 | 14:09:45 |

Which events are **silently dropped** due to the watermark?
code_snippet:
# Watermark threshold at start of this batch:
#   = max_event_time_previous_batch - delay
#   = 14:20:00 - 10 min
#   = 14:10:00
#
# Drop condition: event_time < watermark_threshold  (strictly less than)
#
# e1: 14:25:00  vs  14:10:00
# e2: 14:18:00  vs  14:10:00
# e3: 14:10:00  vs  14:10:00
# e4: 14:09:45  vs  14:10:00
options: e4 only — the drop condition is strictly less than the watermark threshold (14:09:45 < 14:10:00 is true; 14:10:00 < 14:10:00 is false); e3 arrives exactly at the threshold and is retained
e3 and e4 — the watermark boundary is inclusive; events at exactly 14:10:00 are also considered late and dropped
No events are dropped — the watermark only evicts state from completed aggregation windows; it does not filter individual input rows
e2, e3, and e4 — the watermark always retains only events in the last 10 minutes relative to the current wall-clock processing time, not the observed event time
explanation: The watermark threshold = `max_previous_event_time (14:20:00) − delay (10 min) = 14:10:00`. Spark drops events where `event_time < watermark_threshold` — a **strict** less-than comparison. Evaluating each event: e1 (14:25:00 ≥ 14:10:00) retained; e2 (14:18:00 ≥ 14:10:00) retained; e3 (14:10:00 = 14:10:00, not strictly less) retained; e4 (14:09:45 < 14:10:00) dropped. Option B is the most common mistake: the boundary is strictly less than, not less than or equal to — an event arriving exactly at the threshold is not considered late. Option C is wrong — for stateful operators (window aggregations, stream-stream joins), Spark does drop late input rows below the watermark before they enter the state store; the watermark is not purely a state eviction hint. Option D confuses event-time watermarking with processing-time filtering; the watermark threshold is computed from observed event timestamps, not from wall-clock time.
hints: Write out the arithmetic: watermark threshold = max previous event_time − delay. Which of the four events are strictly less than that threshold?
The drop condition is event_time < watermark — strictly less than, not less than or equal to. An event at exactly the threshold is on the boundary, not past it.

title: foreachBatch Driver Crash Mid-Write: What Is in the Output on Restart?
description:
A Structured Streaming job uses `foreachBatch` to append each micro-batch to a Parquet directory. The driver crashes **after writing 60% of batch 7's records** but **before the checkpoint is updated**.

When the job restarts and recovers, what is the state of `/output/events/`?
code_snippet:
def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    (
        batch_df
        .write
        .mode("append")
        .parquet("/output/events/")
    )

query = (
    streaming_df
    .writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/events")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .start()
)
# Driver crashes during batch 7 after writing 60% of records.
# Checkpoint for batch 7 was NOT committed before the crash.
options: The output contains exactly the records written before the crash (60%); Spark detects the partial write via the uncommitted checkpoint and prevents the batch from being replayed
The output directory is empty for the failed batch; Spark rolls back partial Parquet writes when the checkpoint is uncommitted, then replays the full batch cleanly on restart

The output contains duplicate records — the 60% written before the crash plus a full 100% re-write on replay — because the uncommitted checkpoint causes the same source offsets to be re-delivered to write_batch, and append mode writes new files without deduplicating against what already exists
The job fails to restart; an uncommitted checkpoint leaves the checkpoint directory in a corrupt state requiring manual repair before the query can resume
explanation: Structured Streaming's checkpoint records the last **successfully committed** batch ID. Because batch 7's checkpoint was never written, on restart Spark replays the same source offsets (e.g., the same Kafka offset range) and delivers them as batch 7 again. `write_batch` runs a second time with a fresh `batch_df` covering all 100% of the records. The `mode("append")` write appends new Parquet files to `/output/events/` without inspecting or removing the partial files from the failed run. The output now contains the 60% partial files plus a fresh 100% write — approximately 160% of the intended data. `foreachBatch` provides **at-least-once** delivery semantics; the user is responsible for making `write_batch` idempotent, for example by writing to a path keyed by `batch_id` with `mode("overwrite")`, or by using a Delta table that can enforce transactional writes. Option A is wrong — Spark has no mechanism to detect or quarantine partial Parquet files in an external directory. Option B is wrong — Spark does not roll back filesystem writes; the checkpoint and the output path are independently managed. Option D is wrong — an uncommitted checkpoint simply means the last batch will replay; the checkpoint directory structure remains internally consistent.
hints: The checkpoint tracks the last committed batch ID. If batch 7 wasn't committed, what does Spark re-deliver on restart — and what does append mode do when the same data arrives twice?
foreachBatch gives at-least-once guarantees. What responsibility does that place on the write_batch function?

title: Pandas UDF: Predicting Output for Null and Zero Inputs
description: The pandas UDF below is applied to a DataFrame with four rows. What are the four output values for the `log_x` column?
code_snippet:
import math
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@pandas_udf("double")
def safe_log(s: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    return np.log(s)

data = [(1.0,), (None,), (math.e,), (0.0,)]
df = spark.createDataFrame(data, ["x"])
df.select(safe_log(F.col("x")).alias("log_x")).show()
options: 0.0 | null | 1.0 | -Infinity — Spark converts null inputs to NaN before passing to the pandas Series; np.log(NaN) = NaN, which Spark converts back to null on return; np.log(0.0) = -∞, a valid IEEE 754 double that is preserved
0.0 | NaN | 1.0 | null — null is passed as NaN and returned as NaN (not converted back to null); np.log(0.0) raises a domain error that Spark catches and converts to null
0.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 | 0.0 — Spark substitutes 0.0 as a safe default for both null inputs and non-finite results when returning from a DoubleType UDF
AnalysisException at runtime — pandas_udf cannot process nullable DoubleType input; the input column must be cast to a non-nullable type before the UDF executes
explanation: For numeric pandas UDFs, Spark converts **null column values to NaN** before constructing the pandas Series passed to the UDF. Inside the UDF, `np.log(NaN)` propagates NaN (IEEE 754 quiet NaN). When Spark reads the returned Series back into a Spark column, **NaN values are converted back to null** for nullable `DoubleType` results — so the None input row shows null in the output. `np.log(1.0) = 0.0` and `np.log(math.e) = 1.0` are straightforward. `np.log(0.0)` produces `-inf` (IEEE 754 negative infinity): this is a valid double value, not an error, and Spark does **not** convert -inf to null. The four output values are `0.0 | null | 1.0 | -Infinity`. Option B is wrong: Spark does convert NaN back to null on the return path from a pandas UDF — NaN and null are distinct in pandas but are both represented as null in Spark's type system. Option C is wrong: Spark does not substitute 0.0 for nulls or infinities in UDF results. Option D is wrong: pandas UDFs fully support nullable input columns; the null-to-NaN conversion is precisely the mechanism designed to handle them.
hints: Spark uses NaN as the wire format for passing null values into a pandas UDF — and mirrors that in reverse when reading the result back. What does numpy produce for log(NaN), and what does Spark do with NaN on the way back out?
log(0) in IEEE 754 arithmetic is −∞, not an error and not null. Does Spark treat −∞ as a special value for DoubleType columns?

title: Iterative PageRank Crashes with StackOverflowError During Planning
description: A team implements PageRank as a Spark loop. The job runs fine for 10 iterations in testing but crashes in production at iteration 49 with a `StackOverflowError` during query planning — not during execution. The data fits comfortably in cluster memory, and no tasks are launched before the crash.
code_snippet:
spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir("/checkpoints/pagerank")

ranks = graph.vertices.select("id", F.lit(1.0).alias("rank"))

for i in range(50):
    ranks = compute_pagerank_step(ranks, graph.edges)
    # No checkpoint or persist inside the loop
scenario_context:
Driver log — iteration 49 planning phase:
  [INFO]  Analyzing logical plan...
  Exception in thread "main" java.lang.StackOverflowError
    at o.a.spark.sql.catalyst.trees.TreeNode.foreach(TreeNode.scala:187)
    at o.a.spark.sql.catalyst.trees.TreeNode.foreach(TreeNode.scala:187)
    at o.a.spark.sql.catalyst.trees.TreeNode.foreach(TreeNode.scala:187)
    ... (repeated 1,042 times)
    at o.a.spark.sql.catalyst.analysis.Analyzer$$anonfun$execute

Spark UI: no stages launched before the crash
Executor memory at crash time: 12% of capacity
options: The checkpoint directory is on a local filesystem path that executor nodes cannot reach; the StackOverflowError is a misleading Java exception masking a network timeout when Spark tries to write checkpoint metadata

Each loop iteration creates a new DataFrame whose logical plan references the previous ranks DataFrame via Spark's lazy evaluation. After 50 iterations ranks carries a 50-level deep nested plan DAG. Catalyst traverses this plan recursively during analysis; the recursive tree-walk overflows the JVM call stack before a single task is submitted. The fix is to call ranks.checkpoint() (or ranks.localCheckpoint()) every 5–10 iterations to materialise the DataFrame and truncate the lineage to a single node.

The StackOverflowError is caused by Python recursion inside compute_pagerank_step — Spark's py4j bridge serialises Python call frames into the JVM, and 50 nested Python frames exceed the JVM stack limit
spark.sql.optimizer.maxIterations controls plan tree depth; raising it from the default 100 to 500 allows Catalyst to analyse deeper plans without overflowing
explanation: Spark uses **lazy evaluation**: `compute_pagerank_step(ranks, ...)` does not execute immediately — it returns a new DataFrame whose logical plan contains the previous `ranks` plan as a child node. After 50 iterations, `ranks` has a 50-level deep DAG where each node references the prior iteration's plan. When Catalyst analyzes this plan, it traverses the tree **recursively** — the call stack depth equals the plan depth. At 50 iterations with several plan nodes per step, the recursion exceeds the JVM's default stack size (~512–1024 frames) and throws `StackOverflowError`. The fix: call `ranks = ranks.checkpoint()` every 5–10 iterations. `checkpoint()` materialises the DataFrame to disk and returns a new DataFrame with a **truncated, single-node plan** — breaking the lineage chain. `localCheckpoint()` is faster (in-memory only) but does not survive a driver failure. The crash occurs before any tasks launch because it happens during Catalyst analysis, before physical plan construction. Option A is wrong — filesystem access issues produce `IOException`, not `StackOverflowError`, and would fail at the checkpoint call, not during plan analysis. Option C is wrong — py4j uses message passing, not nested JVM call frames; Python recursion does not contribute to the JVM stack. Option D is wrong — `maxIterations` controls how many optimisation rule application passes Catalyst makes, not the depth of the plan tree itself.
hints: No stages launched and the error is inside Catalyst's tree traversal — what is growing with each loop iteration that Catalyst then has to recurse through?
Lazy evaluation means each call to compute_pagerank_step extends the logical plan rather than executing it. After N iterations, how deep is that plan, and how does Catalyst traverse it?

title: Streaming Windows Always Emitted One Full Trigger Cycle Late
description: A Structured Streaming job aggregates clickstream events into 2-minute tumbling windows with a 5-minute watermark. The trigger fires every minute. The ops team observes that window results always appear one full trigger cycle later than expected — the 11:00–11:02 window never emits at 11:02, only at 11:03 or later.
code_snippet:
df_agg = (
    streaming_df
    .withWatermark("event_time", "5 minutes")
    .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "2 minutes"))
    .count()
)

query = (
    df_agg
    .writeStream
    .outputMode("append")
    .format("delta")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/clicks")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .start()
)
scenario_context:
Trigger log (condensed):
  T1 11:01 — max event_time ingested = 11:02:45
              Watermark after T1   = 11:02:45 - 5 min = 10:57:45
              Window 11:00-11:02 end (11:02) > watermark (10:57:45) → NOT released
              Output: 0 windows emitted

  T2 11:02 — max event_time ingested = 11:06:10
              Watermark after T2   = 11:06:10 - 5 min = 11:01:10
              Window 11:00-11:02 end (11:02) > watermark (11:01:10) → NOT released
              Output: 0 windows emitted

  T3 11:03 — max event_time ingested = 11:08:30
              Watermark after T3   = 11:08:30 - 5 min = 11:03:30
              Window 11:00-11:02 end (11:02) < watermark (11:03:30) → RELEASED
              Output: 1 window emitted (11:00-11:02, count = 847)
options: The Delta sink introduces a 1-minute metadata commit delay; switching to Parquet format or lowering delta.checkpointInterval eliminates the lag

In Append output mode a window is emitted only after the watermark has advanced strictly past the window's end time. The watermark advances only when new events with higher event_times arrive — not on wall-clock time. For the 11:00–11:02 window to emit, incoming events must push the watermark past 11:02; that requires event_times above 11:07:00. Even with a 1-minute trigger, no window can be released until a later batch delivers those higher event_times.
processingTime triggers and event-time watermarks are incompatible; the trigger delay compounds the watermark delay multiplicatively and the two must not be used together

The 2-minute window is shorter than the 5-minute watermark delay, which violates a Structured Streaming invariant; windows must be at least as wide as the watermark to guarantee correct emission timing
explanation: In **Append output mode**, a window result is emitted only when the watermark has advanced **strictly past** the window's end time. The watermark = `max observed event_time − watermark delay`. Critically, **the watermark only advances when new events with higher timestamps arrive** — not on wall-clock time, and not because the trigger fires. From the log: after T1 (watermark 10:57:45) and T2 (watermark 11:01:10), the window 11:00–11:02 has end time 11:02, which still exceeds both watermarks — the window cannot emit. Only at T3 do incoming events with event_time=11:08:30 push the watermark to 11:03:30, which finally exceeds 11:02, releasing the window. The one-trigger latency is not a bug — it is the correct behaviour of the watermark + Append mode combination. The latency is determined by how quickly the incoming event stream delivers timestamps high enough to advance the watermark, not by the trigger interval. Option A is wrong — Delta's commit latency is milliseconds; a full trigger-cycle delay means the window genuinely was not ready to emit. Option C is wrong — processingTime triggers and event-time watermarks are fully compatible and are the standard production pattern. Option D is wrong — there is no constraint requiring window duration ≥ watermark delay; the two parameters are independent.
hints: Watermark advancement depends entirely on observed event_time values in incoming batches. What event_time must arrive before the watermark can surpass the 11:02 window end?
Even if the trigger fires every minute, can the watermark advance without new high-timestamp events? What controls how far the watermark moves each batch?
concepts: watermark delay and window release timing

title: Delta MERGE Fails on Large Batch After Consumer Offset Reset
description: A CDC pipeline merges Kafka change events into a Delta table using `foreachBatch`. It ran successfully for weeks processing ~50,000 events per batch. After a Kafka consumer offset reset replayed messages, a 200,000-event batch triggers an `AnalysisException`. Same code, same table.
scenario_context:
Normal operation (50K events/batch):
  MERGE completes in 3 min 10 s — no errors

After consumer offset reset (200K events):
  org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException:
    MERGE statement detected multiple rows matching on the same target row,
    and resulted in an ambiguous update or delete.
    Please update your MERGE statement to limit the number of source rows
    that match a given target row.
    SQLSTATE: 21506

MERGE execution log:
  [INFO]  Source DataFrame: 200,147 rows
  [WARN]  Duplicate user_ids in source: 18,943 user_ids appear 2–5 times each
options: Delta MERGE has an undocumented row-count limit; batches above 100,000 rows must be split into smaller chunks using the batch_id parameter

The offset reset replayed messages, producing multiple change events for the same user_id within a single source batch. The SQL MERGE standard (enforced by Delta) requires each target row to match at most one source row in a whenMatchedUpdate; when multiple source rows match the same target user_id, the update is ambiguous and Delta raises AnalysisException SQLSTATE 21506. The fix: deduplicate batch_df by user_id before the MERGE, keeping only the latest event per user_id (e.g. via a window function ordered by updated_at desc).

The AnalysisException is a schema evolution conflict: replayed Kafka messages used an older Avro schema with extra fields, triggering Delta's schema enforcement and masking as an ambiguous-match error
The error is caused by Delta's transaction log growing too large during the offset reset; running VACUUM before the MERGE resolves the ambiguous-match check
explanation: The SQL MERGE standard requires that each target row match **at most one source row** in a matched UPDATE or DELETE clause — otherwise the result is ambiguous (which of the N matching source rows should determine the final state?). Delta Lake enforces this invariant and raises `AnalysisException SQLSTATE 21506` when it detects violations. During normal operation, Kafka delivered each user_id at most once per batch window, so no conflicts arose. After the consumer offset reset, messages were replayed: 18,943 user_ids appear 2–5 times in the 200K-row batch — one row per replayed message. Each of those user_ids now matches multiple source rows for the same target user_id row, triggering the error. The fix is to deduplicate `batch_df` before the MERGE: `batch_df.withColumn('rn', row_number().over(Window.partitionBy('user_id').orderBy(desc('updated_at')))).filter('rn == 1')` ensures each target row can match at most one source row. Option A is wrong — Delta MERGE has no row-count limit; the error is specifically about duplicate source keys, not batch size. Option C is wrong — schema mismatches produce a different exception (`AnalysisException: A schema mismatch detected`), not SQLSTATE 21506. Option D is wrong — VACUUM manages file retention; it has no effect on MERGE's per-row cardinality check.
hints: The error says 'multiple rows matching the same target row'. What property of the source DataFrame causes this — and what does a consumer offset reset do to the messages in a batch?
MERGE requires a 1-to-1 or many-to-1 relationship from source to target (many source rows can miss, but at most one can match each target row). How do you enforce that?

title: MERGE Scans 798 of 800 Files After 30 Days of Good Pruning
description: A team runs `OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (event_type)` on a Delta table and sees excellent file pruning on day 1. By day 30, the nightly CDC MERGE is scanning nearly the entire table. The table size and MERGE workload are unchanged.
code_snippet:
# One-time optimisation after the table was built
spark.sql("""
    OPTIMIZE user_events
    ZORDER BY (event_type)
""")

# Nightly CDC MERGE — join key is user_id
(
    DeltaTable.forName(spark, "user_events")
    .alias("t")
    .merge(
        df_updates.alias("s"),
        "t.user_id = s.user_id"
    )
    .whenMatchedUpdate(set={"payload": col("s.payload")})
    .execute()
)
scenario_context:
Day 1 (immediately after OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY event_type):
  MERGE duration   : 2 min 18 s
  Files scanned    : 120 / 800
  Skipping log     : event_type min/max statistics eliminated 680 files

Day 30 (no OPTIMIZE or VACUUM since day 1):
  MERGE duration   : 54 min
  Files scanned    : 798 / 800
  Skipping log     : [WARN] No data skipping statistics available for column 'user_id'
                     [INFO] event_type: 6 distinct values, strong Z-order clustering present
options: Delta's Z-order index expires after approximately 30 days; the fix is to increase delta.dataSkippingNumIndexedCols so that statistics are retained for longer

ZORDER BY (event_type) clusters files so each file holds a narrow range of event_type values — giving strong pruning when filtering on event_type. But MERGE joins on user_id, so Delta checks per-file user_id min/max statistics to skip files. Because data was sorted by event_type, user_id values are scattered randomly across all files; each file spans nearly the full user_id range, making file skipping on user_id impossible. Additionally, 30 days of incremental MERGE writes added new files with no ZORDER at all, diluting the original clustering. The fix: re-run OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (user_id) periodically so files are clustered on the actual MERGE predicate column.

The day-30 regression is caused by Delta's auto-compaction writing thousands of small files that overwhelm the transaction log reader; running VACUUM resolves the metadata bloat and restores data skipping

Z-ordering is only effective on columns with high cardinality; event_type has only 6 distinct values, which made the day-1 pruning coincidental; switching to PARTITION BY event_type gives deterministic, permanent pruning
explanation: Delta's data skipping evaluates **per-file min/max statistics** for each column to decide which files can be skipped for a given predicate. `OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY (event_type)` reorders data so that each file contains a narrow band of `event_type` values — files whose `event_type` range doesn't overlap the query filter are eliminated instantly. But the MERGE predicate is `t.user_id = s.user_id`. Delta must check `user_id` min/max per file to prune files that cannot contain matching user_ids. After Z-ordering on `event_type`, user_id values within each file reflect whatever user_ids happened to co-occur with each event_type cluster — there is no clustering on user_id, so each file's user_id min/max spans nearly the full domain. No file can be skipped based on user_id, and MERGE scans everything. The 30-day compounding effect: each nightly MERGE appends new Parquet files written in arbitrary row order with no ZORDER — these new files have full-range user_id statistics as well, growing the unsorted fraction of the table. Fix: run `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (user_id)` periodically to cluster data on the MERGE join key. Option A is wrong — Z-order statistics don't expire; the issue is that the wrong column was clustered. Option C is wrong — VACUUM removes old file versions (for time-travel rollback); it does not affect data skipping statistics on active files. Option D is wrong — Z-ordering is effective on low-cardinality columns (the space-filling curve applies regardless of cardinality); the day-1 pruning on event_type was genuine but served the wrong query pattern.
hints: Delta skips files based on per-file min/max statistics for the column in the filter predicate. Which column does the MERGE predicate filter on — and which column was ZORDER applied to?
After sorting by event_type, what does the distribution of user_id values look like within each file? Can Delta use per-file user_id min/max to eliminate any files?
concepts: Delta data skipping on MERGE predicate

title: 9× Slowdown After Halving Executor Memory Despite Identical Total RAM
description: A cost-optimisation exercise doubles the executor count and halves each executor's memory, keeping total cluster RAM constant. The nightly pipeline goes from 18 minutes to nearly 3 hours. All configuration aside from executor count and memory is unchanged.
code_snippet:
# Pipeline code unchanged
df_result = (
    df_events
    .groupBy("user_id", "session_id")
    .agg(
        F.sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
        F.count("*").alias("event_count")
    )
    .join(df_users,    on="user_id",    how="inner")
    .join(df_sessions, on="session_id", how="inner")
    .filter(col("total_revenue") > 0)
)
df_result.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/output/daily_revenue")

# spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200  (unchanged throughout)
scenario_context:
Before (40 executors × 8 GB, 2 cores each):
  Pipeline duration       : 18 min
  Stage 4 (SortMergeJoin) : 17 min 40 s
  Stage 4 GC time         : 4%
  Stage 4 shuffle spill   : 0 bytes

After (80 executors × 4 GB, 2 cores each):
  Pipeline duration       : 2 h 51 min
  Stage 4 (SortMergeJoin) : 2 h 48 min
  Stage 4 GC time         : 43%
  Stage 4 shuffle spill   : 847 GB

Defaults unchanged:
  spark.memory.fraction        = 0.6
  spark.memory.storageFraction = 0.5
options: With 80 executors and 200 shuffle partitions, 120 executors are idle during Stage 4; the bottleneck is parallelism starvation — raising spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 400 resolves the slowdown regardless of executor memory

Halving executor memory halves the execution memory budget available to each sort task. With 4 GB executors and 2 cores per executor, each active task's execution memory = 4 GB × 0.6 / 2 = 1.2 GB (vs 2.4 GB before). A sort-merge join must sort its shuffle partition in memory; when the data exceeds this budget, Spark spills to disk and performs external merge-sort — reading and writing sorted runs from disk, which is 50–100× slower than in-memory sort. The 847 GB spill confirms nearly every sort operation fell back to disk. Total cluster memory is the same, but per-task sort capacity is halved.

The GC increase from 4% to 43% is caused by running 80 JVM instances simultaneously — stop-the-world GC pauses are synchronised across all executors, and 80 concurrent full-GC events create a cluster-wide pause that the 40-executor cluster never experienced

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=200 is too low for 80 executors; each executor receives only 2.5 partitions on average, creating uneven load distribution that forces most executors to spill while a few are overloaded
explanation: The intuition that 'same total memory = same performance' breaks once per-task execution memory falls below the threshold needed to hold a sort buffer in memory. Execution memory per task = `executor_memory × memory.fraction / concurrent_tasks_per_executor = 4 GB × 0.6 / 2 = 1.2 GB`. Before the change: `8 GB × 0.6 / 2 = 2.4 GB` per task — enough to sort each shuffle partition in memory. After: 1.2 GB per task. A sort-merge join reads one shuffle partition, sorts it in memory, and merges it against the other side. When the sort data exceeds execution memory, Spark spills excess sorted runs to disk and performs **external merge-sort** — writing multiple spill files and reading them back during the merge phase. 847 GB of spill means the vast majority of sort operations went to disk, which is 50–100× slower than in-memory sort. High GC time (43%) is a secondary symptom: repeated allocation and release of sort buffers during spill cycles creates garbage collection pressure. The fix: restore 8 GB executors, reduce `spark.executor.cores` to 1 (doubling per-task memory), or increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to make each partition smaller. Option A is wrong — 200 partitions across 80 executors means 2.5 partitions per executor on average, which is acceptable load distribution; idle executors are not why Stage 4 took 2h 48m. Option C is wrong — JVM GC is per-JVM and not synchronised across the cluster; 80 independent GC cycles do not produce worse total pause time than 40 cycles with the same aggregate heap. Option D conflates partition size with sort spill; raising shuffle.partitions does help if individual partitions are too large, but that is a consequence of executor memory being halved, not an independent cause.
hints: Before and after have identical total RAM but different per-executor amounts. What changes for each individual sort task's memory budget when executor memory is halved?
847 GB of spill means data that previously sorted in memory no longer fits. Trace the execution memory formula: how much memory does each active sort task have with 4 GB executors vs 8 GB?
concepts: total RAM vs per-task memory fallacy

title: Many-to-Many Join Fan-Out: Row Count and OOM Risk
description:
A pipeline joins two non-unique tables:

```python
# user_events: 2M rows
#   user_id has ~200K distinct values (avg 10 rows per user)
#   event_id is unique

# user_labels: 600K rows
#   user_id has ~200K distinct values (avg 3 labels per user)
#   label_id is unique

result = user_events.join(user_labels, on='user_id', how='inner')
result.count()
```

Assuming all 200K `user_id` values appear in both tables, what does `result.count()` return — and what is the primary production risk?
options: 2M — left table grain is preserved in all joins; the right table only filters which rows survive.
600K — the smaller table drives the output cardinality in an inner join.
~2.6M — Spark deduplicates on the join key, limiting output to a value between the two input sizes.

~6M — the join emits one row per matching (event, label) pair per user: 10 events × 3 labels = 30 rows per user × 200K users. The shuffle intermediate materialises all rows for each user_id in a single partition, amplifying data volume and risking executor OOM.
explanation:
When `user_id` is non-unique on **both** sides, the join is many-to-many. Spark emits the Cartesian product of matching rows within each join key group: 10 event rows × 3 label rows = 30 output rows per user_id × 200K users = **6M output rows**.

The critical production risk: during the shuffle, all `user_events` rows AND all `user_labels` rows for the same `user_id` must be co-located in one partition. The intermediate data per partition scales as O(M×N) per key, not O(M+N). This multiplicative growth can cause executor OOM or catastrophic disk spill even when each individual table fits comfortably in memory.

**Option 0** is the most common misconception: left-grain preservation only holds for left-semi joins or aggregations, not plain inner/left joins.

**Option 1** is wrong: inner join cardinality is not bounded by either input; it equals the number of matching pairs.

**Option 2** is wrong: joins never deduplicate output. Deduplication requires an explicit `dropDuplicates()` or `distinct()` call.
hints: user_id appears in avg 10 rows in user_events and avg 3 rows in user_labels. How many output rows does a single user_id produce — is it additive (10+3) or multiplicative (10×3)?

The output is multiplicative. Now consider what happens in the shuffle: all user_events and user_labels rows for a hot user_id must land in the same executor partition simultaneously. What is the memory implication?

title: rangeBetween with Numeric Interval: Which Rows Enter the Frame?
description:
```python
from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import avg

df = spark.createDataFrame([
    ('eng', 80), ('eng', 100), ('eng', 100), ('eng', 130), ('eng', 160),
], ['dept', 'score'])

w = Window.partitionBy('dept').orderBy('score').rangeBetween(-30, 30)

df.withColumn('avg_nearby', avg('score').over(w)).show()
```

For the rows where `score = 100` (either occurrence), what is `avg_nearby`?
options: 100.0 — the frame [score-30, score+30] = [70, 130] is centred on 100; only rows with score exactly 100 fall at the midpoint and are included.
96.67 — the frame [70, 130] includes {80, 100, 100} (130 is excluded because rangeBetween uses a half-open interval, closed at the lower end only).
110.0 — the frame [70, 130] includes {100, 100, 130} (80 is excluded because it falls outside the symmetric ±30 band from 100).
explanation:
`rangeBetween(-30, 30)` on `score=100` defines the value interval [100−30, 100+30] = **[70, 130]**, with **both endpoints inclusive**.

Rows with scores in [70, 130]: 80 ✓ (≥70), 100 ✓, 100 ✓, 130 ✓ (≤130). Score 160 is excluded (>130). Four rows are in the frame.

avg = (80 + 100 + 100 + 130) / 4 = 410 / 4 = **102.5**.

Because `rangeBetween` is value-based, both score=100 rows see the **same** frame and receive the same `avg_nearby`.

**Option 0** is wrong: score=80 satisfies 80 ≥ 70, so it is included. The frame is not limited to the midpoint value.

**Option 2** is wrong: `rangeBetween` uses **closed** intervals on both ends; score=130 satisfies 130 ≤ 130 and is included.

**Option 3** is wrong: score=80 satisfies 80 ≥ 70; it is within the [70, 130] band. The frame lower boundary is inclusive.
hints: rangeBetween(-30, 30) translates to the value interval [score−30, score+30]. For score=100, the interval is [70, 130]. Which of the five scores — 80, 100, 100, 130, 160 — fall inside this interval?
Are the interval endpoints inclusive or exclusive? Verify the boundary scores 80 and 130 individually.

title: pivot() Missing Values: Null Propagation Through Arithmetic
description:
```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

df = spark.createDataFrame([
    ('alice', 'q1', 100), ('alice', 'q2', 200), ('alice', 'q3', 150),
    ('bob',   'q1', 120), ('bob',   'q3', 180),   # bob has no q2
    ('carol', 'q2',  90), ('carol', 'q3', 210),   # carol has no q1
], ['user', 'quarter', 'revenue'])

pivoted = df.groupBy('user').pivot('quarter', ['q1', 'q2', 'q3']).sum('revenue')

result = pivoted \
    .withColumn('h1_revenue', col('q1') + col('q2')) \
    .withColumn('total',      col('q1') + col('q2') + col('q3'))

result.select('user', 'h1_revenue', 'total').show()
```

What are `h1_revenue` and `total` for user **bob**?
options: h1_revenue=120, total=300 — pivot fills missing combinations with 0; arithmetic on 0 proceeds normally.
h1_revenue=null, total=null — pivot fills missing combinations with null, and null propagates through all arithmetic: null+anything=null.
h1_revenue=null, total=300 — the h1 partial sum is null, but Spark falls back to summing only non-null addends for the total.
An AnalysisException is raised — col('q1') + col('q2') fails at plan analysis when either column contains null values.
explanation:
`pivot()` fills missing (user, quarter) combinations with **null**, not 0. Bob has no q2 entry → bob's `q2` column is null after pivot.

Spark arithmetic propagates null: `null + anything = null`. Therefore:
- `h1_revenue = col('q1') + col('q2') = 120 + null = null`
- `total = col('q1') + col('q2') + col('q3') = null + 180 = null`

Both columns are null for bob, despite q1=120 and q3=180 being non-null — the single null in q2 poisons the entire arithmetic chain.

**Option 0** is the classic error: pivot does NOT default to 0. Developers expecting zero-fill must explicitly call `.fillna(0)` on the pivoted DataFrame, or use `coalesce(col('q2'), lit(0))`.

**Option 2** is wrong: there is no partial-null fallback. Null propagation is total in standard arithmetic; Spark follows SQL semantics here.

**Option 3** is wrong: arithmetic on nullable columns does not raise an AnalysisException — it silently returns null, which is precisely the production risk this question highlights.
hints: What value does pivot() assign to a (user, quarter) combination that has no corresponding rows in the source data? Is it 0 or something else?
In Spark SQL, what is the result of any arithmetic expression that includes a null operand? Does that result change if other operands are non-null?

title: Fan-Out Inflation in a CTR Pipeline: Finding the Correct Fix
description:
A pipeline computes per-campaign click-through rate (CTR). `impressions` has one row per impression (`impression_id` unique). `clicks` has one row per click (`click_id` unique). A single impression can generate multiple clicks.

```python
result = (
    impressions
    .join(clicks, on='impression_id', how='left')
    .groupBy('campaign_id')
    .agg(
        count('impression_id').alias('total_impressions'),
        count('click_id').alias('total_clicks'),
        (count('click_id') / count('impression_id')).alias('ctr'),
    )
)
```

Which statement correctly describes the bug and the fix?
options: Nothing is wrong — the left join preserves the impressions grain because impression_id is unique in impressions, so count('impression_id') correctly counts distinct impressions.

total_impressions is over-counted: each impression with k clicks fans out to k rows, so count('impression_id') counts click rows, not impressions. Fix: use countDistinct('impression_id') as the denominator, or compute impression counts before joining.
total_clicks is over-counted: the left join includes impressions with no clicks, and null click_id rows inflate count('click_id') because count() does not skip nulls.
Both counts are equally wrong: the left join produces a Cartesian product between impressions and clicks, inflating both counts by the same factor and keeping CTR correct.
explanation:
Each impression with k clicks fans out to k rows in the joined result. `count('impression_id')` counts every joined row — an impression with 3 clicks is counted 3 times → `total_impressions` is over-stated → CTR denominator is inflated → CTR is under-stated.

`count('click_id')` is correct: it counts non-null click_id values, which equals the total click count (left-join unmatched impressions have null click_id, which count() skips).

**Fixes:** (a) `countDistinct('impression_id')` as the denominator; or (b) pre-aggregate impressions counts before joining: `impressions.groupBy('campaign_id').count()` then join the click summary.

**Option 0** is the core misconception: left join does NOT preserve grain when the right side has multiple matches per key. 'Left join preserves grain' is only true for left-semi joins.

**Option 2** is wrong: `count('click_id')` skips nulls by SQL semantics. Unmatched impression rows (null click_id) are not counted — the click count is correct.

**Option 3** is wrong: this is not a Cartesian product. Impressions are joined to clicks on impression_id; clicks multiply impressions but impressions do not multiply clicks.
hints: When one impression joins to multiple clicks, each impression row duplicates in the result. How does this duplication affect the numerator of your CTR calculation?
count('click_id') skips null values. Left-join unmatched rows have null click_id. Does that make the click count correct or inflated?

title: Debug: rangeBetween on Integer Dates Fails with Data Gaps
description:
An engineer wants a 3-day trailing sum of revenue (today plus the 2 most recent prior days), partitioned by region. The `day` column is stored as Unix day integers (e.g. 19000 = 2022-01-25).

```python
from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum

w = (Window.partitionBy('region').orderBy('day')
           .rangeBetween(-2, 0))

df.withColumn('trailing_3d_revenue', spark_sum('revenue').over(w))
```

In testing on consecutive days (19000, 19001, 19002) the output is correct. In production, data sometimes has date gaps (e.g. 19000, 19005, 19010). The trailing sum for day 19010 unexpectedly contains only that single day's revenue, not the preceding 2 days. What is the root cause and correct fix?
options: The partitionBy on 'region' is incorrect — it splits the window at region boundaries, which prevents the rolling sum from spanning consecutive days correctly.

rangeBetween(-2, 0) uses the ORDER BY column's numeric value as the frame boundary. On day=19010, the frame covers days in the value range [19008, 19010], which contains no other rows when the preceding days are 19000 and 19005. Fix: use rowsBetween(-2, 0) to include the 2 preceding physical rows regardless of their day values.
rangeBetween(-2, 0) defines a 2-row lookback, identical to rowsBetween(-2, 0). The bug is that the day column must be cast to DateType before window functions can use it correctly.
The window needs an explicit orderBy('day', 'region') to prevent Spark from reordering rows arbitrarily within the partition.
explanation:
`rangeBetween(-2, 0)` interprets the boundaries as **numeric offsets on the ORDER BY column value**, not as a count of preceding rows. For day=19010, the frame is the value range [19010−2, 19010+0] = **[19008, 19010]**. Since no rows have day values in [19008, 19009], only the day=19010 row itself is included — the '3-day window' contains exactly 1 row.

The test on consecutive days passed because rangeBetween(-2, 0) on sequential integers happens to match the 2 preceding physical rows. The bug is invisible until data has gaps.

**Fix:** `rowsBetween(-2, 0)` includes the 2 preceding physical rows regardless of their day values — which is the intended '3-day lookback' semantics.

**Option 0** is wrong: `partitionBy('region')` is correct; it scopes the window per region. It does not cause the rolling-sum failure.

**Option 2** is wrong: `rangeBetween` and `rowsBetween` have fundamentally different semantics — `rangeBetween` is value-based, `rowsBetween` is position-based. Casting to DateType does not change this.

**Option 3** is wrong: ordering by multiple columns is not the issue; the ORDER BY is already correct.
hints: rangeBetween uses numeric arithmetic on the ORDER BY column value. For day=19010 and rangeBetween(-2, 0), what is the value interval [19010+(-2), 19010+0]? Which of the data rows — 19000, 19005, 19010 — fall inside it?
rowsBetween counts physical row positions, not column value differences. Which frame type gives a stable '2 preceding rows' window regardless of gaps between day values?

title: explode vs explode_outer: Which Preserves All Users in the Pipeline?
description:
A pipeline enriches user tags with reference metadata, then counts processed users as a completeness check:

```python
# users: user_id, tags (ArrayType — can be null or [])  
# tag_metadata: tag, category, priority

# Option A
result_a = (
    users.select('user_id', explode('tags').alias('tag'))
    .join(tag_metadata, on='tag', how='inner')
)

# Option B
result_b = (
    users.select('user_id', explode_outer('tags').alias('tag'))
    .join(tag_metadata, on='tag', how='left')
)

# Downstream: count distinct users processed
result.groupBy('user_id').count()
```

A downstream `groupBy('user_id').count()` is used to verify completeness. Which statement is correct?
options: Option A is preferable — inner join with explode is the most efficient pattern; it guarantees every output tag has a metadata match and keeps the result clean.
Both options produce the same user_id count downstream — explode vs explode_outer only changes the number of rows per user, not which users appear.

Option A silently drops users with null or empty tags from the downstream count, because explode() emits no rows for null/empty arrays. Option B preserves them via explode_outer() and a left join. If the completeness check must include all users, Option B is correct.
Option B is correct only when all tags are guaranteed to have matching metadata — otherwise, the left join emits null metadata rows that corrupt category and priority columns.
explanation:
`explode()` emits zero output rows for null or empty arrays — users with no tags entirely disappear from `result_a`. They are invisible to the downstream `groupBy('user_id').count()`, so the completeness check silently under-counts processed users.

`explode_outer()` emits one row with `tag=null` for null/empty arrays. The subsequent left join on `tag=null` finds no match in `tag_metadata` — the user's category and priority columns are null, but the user's `user_id` row is still present. The completeness count is correct.

**Option 0** is wrong on both claims: 'inner join guarantees metadata match' only for tags *that have metadata entries* — unmatched tags are silently dropped. 'Most efficient' is irrelevant if correctness requires preserving all users.

**Option 1** is wrong: whether a user has 0 tags determines whether they appear in `result_a` at all. explode() and explode_outer() produce different user sets for tag-less users.

**Option 3** is wrong about Option B's scope: a left join handles unmatched tags by producing null metadata columns — it does not corrupt the result. The concern about 'only when all tags match' applies to inner join (Option A), not left join.
hints: A user with tags=[] (empty array): how many rows does explode() emit for them? How many does explode_outer() emit?
After explode(), a tag-less user contributes 0 rows to the pipeline. What does that mean for their appearance in the downstream groupBy('user_id').count()?

title: AQE Skew-Join Enabled but groupBy Outlier Task Not Split
description: A daily pipeline aggregates 2 TB of events: `events.groupBy('user_id').agg(F.count().alias('cnt'))`. Stage 4 (the groupBy shuffle reduce) shows 1000 tasks; median task: 3 min. One outlier task has been reading for 5 hours and processed 280 GB — all rows for `user_id='bot_crawler'`. `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`. `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true`. The Spark UI confirms AQE is active but the outlier task was never split.
options: The outlier exceeds `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (default 256 MB) but the partition factor check (5× median size) failed because the median task size is >56 GB — raise the factor to a lower value.
AQE's skew-join optimisation applies only to join shuffle stages; a standalone `groupBy` aggregation shuffle is not a join and cannot be split by the skew-join handler regardless of configuration.
AQE partition coalescing merged the 1000 output partitions into fewer large partitions before the outlier was detected, making the threshold check pass too late to trigger splitting.

The outlier partition is undetected because `bot_crawler` maps to a shuffle partition that also contains millions of other user_ids; AQE skips partitions where the hot key accounts for less than 50% of the rows.
explanation:
AQE's `skewJoin` optimisation detects skew in the **join** stage's shuffle inputs and rewrites the join plan to split the skewed partition. It does not apply to `groupBy` aggregation shuffles — there is no join for it to rewrite. Regardless of how large the outlier aggregation partition is, `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` cannot split it.

Option 0 is wrong: the median task size is ~3 min / roughly 2 GB (2 TB / 1000 partitions ≈ 2 GB per partition). The outlier is 280 GB = 140× the median — far above the 5× factor and 256 MB threshold. Both checks pass easily; they are not the blocker.

Option 2 is wrong: AQE coalesces shuffle partitions for the *output* of a stage, affecting downstream stages. It does not prevent skew detection in the current reduce stage.

Option 3 is wrong: AQE's detection is based on the total byte size of a shuffle partition (map output size), not the concentration of one key within that partition. A single user_id dominating a 280 GB partition would absolutely be detected — but detection is irrelevant when the handler is the wrong kind (join-only).

Fix: salt the `groupBy` key. Add a random salt column (0–49), group by `(user_id, salt)` to spread `bot_crawler` across 50 partitions, then sum the partial counts in a second pass.
hints: AQE has separate optimisations for different plan nodes. Which specific plan node does `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled` target?
The outlier easily meets both the factor and threshold checks. If it's detected, what prevents the split from happening?

title: Salt Fixed the groupBy — Now Downstream Join Is the Bottleneck at 10× Scale
description: After applying a salt-based fix (salt range 0–49), the groupBy finishes in 12 min at 2 TB. At 10× scale (20 TB) the groupBy still completes in acceptable time (salt distributes the load), but the downstream step — `agg_result.join(campaign_metadata, 'user_id')` where `campaign_metadata` is 800 rows — now takes 3.5 hours. At 2 TB scale this join took 8 min. AQE is enabled. The job plan shows a sort-merge join.
options: At 10× scale the salted `agg_result` has 10× more output partitions, so the sort-merge join shuffles 10× more data; use `coalesce` on `agg_result` before the join to reduce shuffle volume.
At 10× scale AQE's broadcast conversion has been disabled by a cluster admin; re-enable `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` explicitly for this session.
At 10× scale `campaign_metadata` (800 rows) still fits in memory on every executor; add an explicit `broadcast(campaign_metadata)` hint to force a broadcast hash join regardless of size estimates.
At 10× scale the sort-merge join's sort phase dominates; add a `repartition('user_id')` before the join so data is pre-partitioned and the sort phase is eliminated.
explanation:
After the salted two-pass groupBy, the final `agg_result` is one row per `user_id` — the same cardinality as the original aggregation, regardless of scale. The join's sort-merge overhead scales with how many bytes need to be shuffled. At 10× input scale the output of the groupBy is also larger (more distinct user_ids), and AQE's size estimate for `campaign_metadata` (800 rows) relative to the now-larger `agg_result` may cause the planner to choose SMJ.

But `campaign_metadata` is 800 rows — it trivially fits in broadcast memory at any scale. The correct fix is to add an explicit `broadcast(campaign_metadata)` hint; this bypasses AQE's size-estimate logic and forces a broadcast hash join, eliminating the entire shuffle for the `campaign_metadata` side.

Option 0 is wrong: `coalesce` on `agg_result` reduces the number of output files (good for write) but does not reduce the shuffle bytes in the join — Spark will still shuffle both sides to align join keys.

Option 1 is wrong: `spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` is a valid config, but `campaign_metadata` at 800 rows is well within any broadcast threshold (default 10 MB); this is not an admin-disabled issue. The real problem is that AQE's runtime size estimate for `campaign_metadata` may be artificially inflated by join-side statistics at scale.

Option 3 is wrong: `repartition('user_id')` pre-aligns the data but Spark still performs a shuffle to co-locate join keys; the sort phase is not eliminated and you pay a full shuffle anyway.
hints: The `campaign_metadata` table is 800 rows at 2 TB scale and still 800 rows at 20 TB scale. What join strategy is always optimal for a table this small?
When AQE's size estimates cause an incorrect join strategy, what takes precedence — a session-level config or an explicit per-query hint?

title: Salted groupBy for count_distinct: Will the Output Be Correct?
description:
After fixing the skew, a colleague extends the pipeline to also compute distinct session counts per user:

```python
df = events.withColumn('salt', (F.rand() * 50).cast('int'))
step1 = df.groupBy('user_id', 'salt').agg(
    F.count_distinct('session_id').alias('distinct_sessions')
)
result = step1.groupBy('user_id').agg(
    F.sum('distinct_sessions').alias('total_sessions')
)
```

`events` has 500 M rows across 8 M users. A single user may have multiple events per session. The colleague claims `total_sessions` will match `events.groupBy('user_id').agg(F.count_distinct('session_id'))`. Is this correct, and why?
options: Correct — `count_distinct` within each `(user_id, salt)` bucket counts a session_id only once per bucket, and summing distinct counts across salt buckets for the same user_id gives the correct total distinct session count.

Incorrect — a session_id that has events with different salt values will be counted as distinct in multiple `(user_id, salt)` buckets; summing those counts overcounts sessions that span more than one salt bucket for the same user.

Incorrect — `F.rand()` assigns salt at the row level; two rows for the same session_id within the same executor partition will always get different salts, so every session_id is split and the count is exactly doubled.
Correct — `count_distinct` is a holomorphic aggregation; Spark's catalyst optimizer automatically detects the salting pattern and rewrites the plan to produce a globally correct distinct count.
explanation:
The result is **incorrect**. `count_distinct` is not additively decomposable across arbitrary subsets. A single `session_id` may appear in multiple events for the same `user_id`, each event receiving a different random `salt` value. That session_id will therefore be counted as a distinct value in every `(user_id, salt)` bucket it appears in. Summing those per-bucket distinct counts overcounts sessions that span more than one salt value.

Example: user_id='u1' has session_id='s1' with 3 events getting salts 0, 7, and 23. step1 counts 's1' as distinct in buckets (u1, 0), (u1, 7), and (u1, 23). Summing gives 3 — but there is only 1 distinct session.

Option 0 is wrong: summing distinct counts from different buckets is only correct if the buckets are disjoint by the distinct dimension — which they are not here (same session_id can appear in multiple salt buckets).

Option 2 is wrong: `rand()` is applied at the row level, but the exact salt values are random — two rows for the same session within the same partition can get the same or different salts; there is no 'exactly doubled' guarantee.

Option 3 is wrong: Catalyst has no such pattern rewriting for arbitrary salt-based `count_distinct`. Holomorphic aggregations (count, sum, min, max) decompose across subsets, but `count_distinct` is explicitly non-holomorphic.

Correct fix: salt only works for `count()` and `sum()`. For `count_distinct`, either (a) move the distinct computation to the second pass: `step1 = df.groupBy('user_id','salt').agg(F.collect_set('session_id'))` then deduplicate, or (b) run the distinct count without salting and accept that that stage is single-threaded for hot users.
hints: Salt distributes rows randomly. Can two rows with the same session_id end up in different salt buckets for the same user?
Which types of aggregations are safe to split across arbitrary subsets and sum? Is `count_distinct` in that category?

title: Pandas UDF vs mapPartitions: Memory and Serialisation Trade-offs
description: A data science team wraps a scikit-learn scoring model in a UDF applied to 50 M rows. Current approach: a `@pandas_udf` that receives a `pd.Series` per column. The job OOMs executors (8 GB each, 4 cores each). A team member proposes switching to `mapPartitions` with a regular Python iterator. Which assessment of the trade-offs is most accurate for this OOM scenario?
options: Switching to `mapPartitions` is strictly worse: it serialises rows one at a time via pickle, increasing per-row overhead and peak memory versus the Arrow-based batch transfer in pandas UDF.

The pandas UDF transfers all columns of a partition to the Python process at once via Arrow; for wide rows and large partitions this can double peak memory (JVM + Python). `mapPartitions` with a streaming iterator avoids materialising the full partition in Python at once.
The OOM is caused by Arrow IPC serialisation overhead, not data volume; disabling Arrow (`spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled=false`) and using a scalar UDF eliminates the excess memory.
pandas UDF batches are bounded by `spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch`; reducing this to 1000 rows per batch will prevent OOM without changing the UDF architecture.
explanation:
A `@pandas_udf` transfers an entire partition's column data from the JVM to the Python process via Apache Arrow IPC. If the partition is large and the DataFrame has many columns, the Arrow buffer + the resulting `pd.Series` objects can live simultaneously, roughly doubling peak memory: the JVM holds the partition while Arrow copies it to Python, then Python processes it. With 8 GB executors and 4 cores sharing the heap, this easily causes OOM.

`mapPartitions` with a streaming iterator yields rows one at a time to Python (or in small chunks if you batch manually), so the Python process never materialises the entire partition at once. This trades Arrow's efficient columnar transfer for lower peak memory. For this OOM scenario, peak memory reduction is the priority — `mapPartitions` is the right lever.

Option 0 is wrong: `mapPartitions` does not use pickle row-by-row by default; PySpark serialises entire partitions (not rows) across the pipe. The claim that it's 'strictly worse' ignores the peak-memory benefit.

Option 2 is wrong: disabling Arrow switches pandas UDF to row-at-a-time pickle serialisation, which is slower and still materialises data on both sides — it typically *increases* total memory usage and latency.

Option 3 is partially correct but insufficient: reducing `maxRecordsPerBatch` reduces per-batch peak memory but the partition is still fully materialised in the JVM before batching begins. For very large partitions the JVM side alone can OOM before any batch is sent.
hints: A pandas UDF receives a `pd.Series` representing an entire column of a partition. Where does that data live before and after the Arrow transfer?
What does 'streaming iterator' mean for memory in `mapPartitions` vs receiving a complete Series in a pandas UDF?

title: Z-Ordering the Wrong Column: Why File Skipping Doesn't Trigger
description: A Delta table stores 10 TB of clickstream data. Analysts run queries that filter almost exclusively by `user_segment` (10 distinct values; roughly equal row distribution). The table was Z-ordered on `event_timestamp` last week. Queries still scan all 12,000 files. A platform engineer proposes Z-ordering on `user_segment` instead. What is the most accurate prediction of whether this will help?
options: Z-ordering on `user_segment` will not help because Z-ordering works on continuous numeric ranges and `user_segment` is a low-cardinality string column; file skipping only applies to numeric columns with natural ordering.

Z-ordering on `user_segment` will cluster files by segment value, enabling Delta's file-skipping to eliminate ~90% of files for a single-segment filter, but effectiveness is limited because 10 equal-sized segments means at best 90% file elimination per query.

Z-ordering on `user_segment` with 10 equally distributed values will produce files where each file contains all 10 segment values (because Z-ordering co-locates rows with similar multi-dimensional coordinates, not single-dimension values); file skipping will not improve over the current state.

Z-ordering on `event_timestamp` already implicitly clusters by `user_segment` if segment is correlated with timestamp (e.g. segment assignment is time-windowed); re-Z-ordering on segment will have no additional benefit.
explanation:
Z-ordering on `user_segment` will cluster files by segment value: rows with the same `user_segment` are co-located in the same files. Delta's file-level min/max statistics will record `user_segment=segment_A` in a file's column stats; a `WHERE user_segment = 'X'` query can skip every file whose min/max range for `user_segment` excludes 'X'.

With 10 equally distributed segments and good Z-ordering, approximately 10% of files will contain each segment. A single-segment filter skips ~90% of files — a 10× scan reduction. This is a substantial improvement despite the low cardinality.
